new.title: Pipes & Cisterns
sample: This topic was split out of **Time & Work** so that pipes can be learnt on their own. Its paper counts and timed drills are in that topic's Quick revision tab (9 of its 25 IBPS Clerk questions were pipes); four more pipe questions were found in the sister papers (SBI Clerk Sep 2025 twice, IBPS RRB Clerk Dec 2025, IBPS PO Aug 2025).
revision: **One idea:** the tank is a number of units (the LCM of the times). Filling pipes add units, emptying pipes take them away.
| fill and empty together | add fillers, subtract emptiers, divide |
| with a leak it takes longer | leak = pipe alone - pipe with leak |
| all three, and two of them | the missing pipe = all - the pair |
| three times as fast, 50% more efficient | units per hour 3 : 1, 3 : 2 |
| closed after a while / opened late | units stage by stage |
| in turns | units per cycle; stop early if one pipe empties |
| n identical pipes | pipes x time = the tank |
| litres | find where units meet litres: that sizes one unit |
**Traps.** Starting partly full. Asking for the time to empty. A negative net rate means the tank never fills.

intro: A pipe filling a tank is a worker doing a job; a pipe or leak that empties it is a worker undoing the job. Give the tank a number of units, and every question becomes adding and subtracting units per hour.
There are eight short lessons. Three are taken from Time & Work; five are new. Go in order the first time. If Time & Work's first lesson (turning a job into units) is new to you, do it first.
What the papers ask (Time & Work Stage A count plus the sister papers, all memory-based):
| Fill and empty together (W1) | Confirmed, 5 papers | PC1 |
| A missing pipe or a leak (W2) | Confirmed, 5 papers | PC2 |
| Opened or closed partway (W4) | Confirmed, 2 papers | PC4 (two lessons) |
| Fast and slow pipes (W3) | Seen once | PC3 |
| Turns, many pipes, litres | Bank only | PC5, PC6, PC7 |
after: That is the whole topic. The **Quick revision** tab has the table of what to do for each wording.
Time & Work keeps its own pipe lessons as well; the two topics share their practice questions.

lessons.title: Pipes and tanks: the same idea
lessons.plain: New: pipes filling a tank are workers. A pipe that empties the tank is a worker who undoes the work.
teach: A pipe that fills a tank in 20 minutes is just a worker who finishes a job in 20 minutes. So everything from the last lesson carries over: give the tank a number of units, find each pipe's units per minute (or per hour), and add.
There is one new thing. Some pipes **empty** the tank. An emptying pipe, an outlet, a drain or a leak takes water away, so its units are **subtracted**.
Pipe A fills a tank in 6 hours. Pipe B empties it in 10 hours. Both are open.
- Call the tank 30 units.
- A adds 5 units an hour. B removes 3 units an hour.
- Each hour the tank gains 5 - 3 = 2 units.
- Time to fill = 30 / 2 = 15 hours.
If the tank's size is given in **litres**, you do not need to invent units: the litres are the units. A 240-litre tank filled by a pipe in 16 hours gets 240 / 16 = 15 litres an hour from it.
And if the tank is **already partly full**, only the empty part is the job. A half-full tank of 30 units has 15 units left to fill.

example.q: Pipes A and B can fill a tank in 12 hours and 15 hours. Pipe C can empty the full tank in 20 hours. If all three are opened together, how long will the empty tank take to fill?
steps: Call the tank 60 units: 12, 15 and 20 all go into 60.
A adds 5 an hour, B adds 4 an hour, and C removes 3 an hour.
Each hour the tank gains 5 + 4 - 3 = 6 units.
Time = 60 / 6 = 10 hours.

check.q: A pipe can fill a tank in 8 hours and an outlet can empty it in 24 hours. If both are open, in how many hours will the empty tank be full?
check.why: Call the tank 24 units. The pipe adds 3 an hour and the outlet removes 1, so the tank gains 2 an hour. 24 / 2 = 12 hours. (6 hours would be right if both pipes were filling.)

lessons.title: Leaks and drain pipes
lessons.plain: New: last lesson's subtraction, with tanks. The missing one is a leak or a drain.
teach: "A pipe can fill a tank in 12 hours. Because of a leak, it takes 18 hours." The leak is a hidden worker who undoes some of the pipe's work. You find it exactly as you found the missing person in the last lesson.
- Call the tank 36 units.
- The pipe alone adds 36 / 12 = 3 units an hour.
- With the leak, the tank gains only 36 / 18 = 2 units an hour.
- So the leak removes 3 - 2 = 1 unit an hour.
- A full tank of 36 units would drain through the leak in 36 hours.
Read these questions as "what the pipes should add" against "what the tank actually gains". The gap is the drain.
The disguises are the same as for people:
- a third pipe C that is "also open", where the tank fills more slowly than A and B alone would manage, so C must be emptying;
- two outlets, one of them known;
- three pairs of pipes;
- a last line that asks about **half** the tank or some other part.

example.q: A pipe can fill a tank in 10 hours. Because of a leak in the bottom, it takes 15 hours. If the tank is full, how long will the leak take to empty it?
steps: Call the tank 30 units.
The pipe alone adds 3 units an hour.
With the leak the tank gains 30 / 15 = 2 units an hour.
So the leak removes 3 - 2 = 1 unit an hour.
A full tank is 30 units: the leak empties it in 30 hours.

check.q: Pipes A and B together can fill a tank in 4 hours. When a drain pipe C is also open, the tank fills in 6 hours. In how many hours can C alone empty the full tank?
check.why: Call the tank 12 units. A and B add 3 an hour; with C open the tank gains 2. So C removes 1 an hour and empties 12 units in 12 hours.

tags: A leak slows one pipe down.
A third pipe that turns out to be emptying.
The same, and it asks about half the tank.
Two outlets, one of them known.
Three pairs of pipes.
All three, minus a pair; then part of the tank.
A leak: the plainest form.

lessons.title: Fast and slow pipes
lessons.plain: New: one pipe is described by how much faster it is than another, not by its own time.
teach: "A is three times as fast as B" gives the units per hour straight away: A 3, B 1. "B is 50% more efficient than A" gives A 2, B 3.
Then add as usual: together 4 units a minute. If together they take 12 minutes, the tank is 48 units, and A alone takes 48 / 3 = 16 minutes.
A ratio of efficiencies works the same way: "(A and B together) : C = 9 : 2". Find A and B's units from their times, then C from the ratio.
"A takes 5 hours less than B; together they take 6 hours." No pipe's time is given, so **try the options**: together time = product / sum. A = 10, B = 15: 150 / 25 = 6. It fits.
Checked papers: IBPS Clerk 2021 set one.

example.q: Pipe A is twice as fast as pipe B. Together they fill a tank in 10 hours. How long does B alone take?
steps: A 2 units an hour, B 1: together 3.
Tank = 3 x 10 = 30 units.
B alone: 30 / 1 = 30 hours.

check.q: Pipe A fills a tank in 24 minutes. Pipe B is 50% more efficient than A. How long does B take alone?
check.why: B does 1.5 times A's work per minute, so B takes 24 / 1.5 = 16 minutes. (36 makes B slower, not faster.)

tags: A ratio of efficiencies.
"Three times as fast".
Percent words.
No time given: try the options.

lessons.title: Pipes opened and closed at different times
lessons.plain: New: the stages idea with tanks. A pipe is closed early, or opened late.
teach: Stages work the same way for tanks. A pipe being **closed** is a worker leaving; a pipe being **opened later** is a worker joining. Find the units added in each stage and subtract from the tank.
Two forms are particular to pipes.

**"After how many minutes should B be closed so that the tank is full in exactly 9 minutes?"** Look at it from pipe A's side. A is open for all 9 minutes, so you know exactly how much A adds. Whatever is still missing must come from B, and B's units per minute tell you how long B needs to be open.
**A drain that is closed, or opened, partway.** While the drain is open its units are subtracted; once it is closed, they are not. Treat the two stretches as two stages with different net units.
Pipe questions more often ask for the **total** time than work questions do, so remember to add the first stage back at the end when the question says "in how many hours in total".

example.q: Pipes A and B can fill a tank in 12 minutes and 18 minutes. Both are opened together, and after 4 minutes A is closed. In how many more minutes will B fill the tank?
steps: Call the tank 36 units. A adds 3 a minute and B adds 2.
Stage one: 5 a minute for 4 minutes = 20 units.
Units left: 36 - 20 = 16.
Stage two: B alone adds 2 a minute. 16 / 2 = 8 minutes.

check.q: Pipe A can fill a tank in 10 hours and pipe B in 15 hours. A is opened first, and after 5 hours B is also opened. In how many hours in total is the tank full?
check.why: Call the tank 30 units. A adds 3 an hour: 15 units in 5 hours. The other 15 are filled by both at 5 an hour, which takes 3 hours. Total 5 + 3 = 8 hours. (3 is only the second stage.)

tags: Both open, then one is closed.
The same, with an answer that is not a whole number.
One pipe is opened late, and it asks for the total time.
When should a pipe be closed?
A drain that is closed partway.

lessons.title: Harder timings
lessons.plain: New: pipes opened at different clock times, or a question that gives the finish and asks about the start.
teach: Keep the habit from the last lesson: **units added in each stretch of time**, stretch by stretch.
**Opened at 3 pm, 4 pm and 5 pm.** Work out what is in the tank at each clock time, then let the full set run.
**Used for half the time, then together for the other half.** Call the half-time t: units = (B's rate + both rates) x t.
**Closed after a while, and the rest takes so long.** Work out the part done first; the rest tells you the remaining pipes' combined rate. Subtract to find the closed pipe.
Watch the direction: with an emptying pipe in the set, the question may ask when the tank becomes **empty**, not full.

example.q: Pipes A and B fill a tank in 12 and 18 minutes. A is opened at 10:00, B at 10:03. When is the tank full?
steps: Tank = 36 units: A 3, B 2 a minute.
10:00 to 10:03: A adds 9. 27 units are left.
Together 5 a minute: 27 / 5 = 5.4 minutes. Full at about 10:08:24.

check.q: Pipes A and B fill a tank in 20 and 30 minutes. Both are opened; after 6 minutes A is closed. How long does B take to finish?
check.why: Tank 60 units: A 3, B 2. Six minutes together: 30. B finishes the other 30 in 15 minutes. (12 counts only A's 6 minutes.)

tags: Half the time alone, half together.
Find the closed pipe.
A drain opened late.
Clock times, and the tank empties.

lessons.title: Pipes opened in turns
lessons.plain: New: pipes take turns, one hour (or minute) each.
teach: Treat each pair of turns as one **cycle**. Units in one cycle = A's units + B's units.
Take as many full cycles as fit, then finish the rest turn by turn in the starting order.
**With an emptying pipe, stop early.** The tank can fill partway through a filling turn, before the emptying turn comes. So check: after k cycles, can the next filling turn finish it?

A fills in 10 minutes and B empties in 15, in turns from A. Tank 30 units: A +3, B -2, so each 2-minute cycle adds 1. After 27 cycles (54 minutes) the level is 27, and A's next minute takes it to 30: full at 55 minutes, not 60.
No paper in the sample set this with pipes; the work version (alternate days) is in Time & Work.

example.q: Pipes A and B fill a tank in 8 and 12 hours. They are opened in turns, one hour each, starting with A. How long does the tank take?
steps: Tank = 24 units: A 3, B 2. One 2-hour cycle adds 5.
4 cycles (8 hours) add 20. 4 units are left.
A's next hour adds 3, then B needs half an hour for the last 1: 9.5 hours.

check.q: Pipes A and B fill a tank in 6 and 3 hours. In turns of 1 hour each, starting with A, how long does it take?
check.why: Tank 6 units: A 1, B 2, a cycle adds 3. Two cycles fill it exactly: 4 hours. (4.5 adds an extra half turn that is not needed.)

tags: Two filling pipes.
One fills, one empties: stop early.

more.q: Pipes A and B fill a tank in 4 and 6 hours. Opened in turns, one hour each, starting with B, how long does it take?
more.why: Tank 12 units: B 2, A 3, a cycle adds 5. Two cycles (4 hours) give 10; B's next hour adds the last 2: 5 hours. (4 hours 40 minutes lets A take the fifth turn.)

lessons.title: Many identical pipes
lessons.plain: New: the question counts pipes instead of naming them.
teach: Identical pipes are like identical workers: **pipes x time = the tank** (in pipe-minutes).
12 pipes take 40 minutes: the tank is 480 pipe-minutes. With 10 pipes: 48 minutes.
**More pipes opened partway:** half the tank by one pipe, the other half by four pipes, takes a quarter of the time.
**A mix of inlets and outlets:** write the net units per hour with the number of inlets as the unknown, and match it to the time given.

example.q: 8 identical pipes fill a tank in 45 minutes. How long do 6 such pipes take?
steps: The tank is 8 x 45 = 360 pipe-minutes.
360 / 6 = 60 minutes.

check.q: One pipe fills a tank in 8 hours. After half the tank is filled, one more such pipe is opened. How long does the whole tank take?
check.why: Half by one pipe: 4 hours. The other half by two pipes: 2 hours. Total 6. (4 hours forgets the first half was slower.)

tags: Some pipes out of order.
More pipes opened at half.
How many are inlets?

lessons.title: Tanks in litres
lessons.plain: New: some rates are given in litres, so the tank has a real size.
teach: Keep using units, and look for the one place where **units meet litres**. That fixes the size of one unit.

Two pipes fill in 20 and 24 minutes; a waste pipe drains 3 litres a minute; all three fill in 15 minutes. Tank = 120 units: pipes 6 and 5, all three 8, so the waste pipe takes 3 units a minute. Those 3 units are 3 litres: one unit is one litre, and the tank holds 120 litres.
If every rate is already in litres, just subtract and divide: 12 in, 4 out, net 8 a minute; 480 litres takes 60 minutes.
Checked papers: IBPS Clerk 2016 ended a pipes question with a litres step (that question is in the first lesson).

example.q: A leak empties a full tank in 6 hours. An inlet adds 4 litres a minute; with both open, the full tank empties in 8 hours. What is the capacity?
steps: Tank = 24 units: the leak takes 4 an hour; with the inlet the net loss is 3 an hour.
So the inlet adds 1 unit an hour, which is 4 x 60 = 240 litres.
The tank is 24 x 240 = 5,760 litres.

check.q: A tap adds 15 litres a minute and an outlet drains 5 litres a minute. How long to fill an empty 600-litre tank?
check.why: Net 10 litres a minute: 600 / 10 = 60. (40 ignores the outlet.)

tags: Rates already in litres.
Inlet in litres, leak in hours.
A waste pipe in litres.
A leak found from the delay.
